Our climate target

In tackling climate change, the focus is increasingly on limiting the global temperature rise to 1.5° Celsius. Shell supports this ambition.

Our climate target

Achieving net-zero emissions is part of our Powering Progress strategy. Our target is to become a net-zero emissions energy business by 2050. Find out more about how we are working to achieve this target and our progress so far.

Tackling climate change is an urgent challenge. We want to contribute to a net-zero world where any greenhouse gas emissions entering the atmosphere are balanced by removal out of the atmosphere.

That is why we have set a target to become a net-zero emissions energy business by 2050. This supports the more ambitious goal of the UN Paris Agreement: to limit the rise in average global temperature this century to 1.5° Celsius compared to pre-industrial levels.

Our target

Our target is to become a net-zero emissions energy business by 2050.

This means net-zero carbon emissions from our operations – our Scope 1 and 2 emissions – and net zero from the end use of all the energy products we sell – the Scope 3 emissions we report – which account for over 90% of the total emissions reported.

Reduce our absolute emissions by 50% by 2030, compared to 2016 levels on a net basis. This covers all emissions in Scope 1, which come directly from our operations, and Scope 2, from the energy we buy to run our operations.

By 2025, eliminate routine flaring of natural gas, which generates carbon emissions, from our upstream operations.1

Maintain methane emissions intensity below 0.2% by 2025 and achieve near-zero methane emissions by 2030.

Our progress

By the end of 2022, we reduced our absolute emissions from our operations by 30% compared to 2016.

We met our target to keep methane emissions intensity below 0.2% in 2022. Our overall methane emissions intensity was 0.05% for facilities with marketing gas and 0.01% for facilities without marketing gas.

As another way to measure our progress, we have set short-, medium- and long-term targets to reduce the carbon intensity of the energy products we sell.

Net carbon intensity2 measures emissions associated with each unit of energy we sell. It reflects changes in sales of oil and gas products, and changes in sales of low- and zero-carbon products and services — such as biofuels, hydrogen and renewable electricity.

We are aiming to reduce our net carbon intensity by the following amounts over the following periods, compared to a 2016 baseline:

2-3% by 2021 - achieved
3-4% by 2022 - achieved
6-8% by 2023
9-12% by 2024
9-13% by 2025
20% by 2030
45% by 2035
100% by 2050

Our approach

To decarbonise our operations, we are:

making portfolio changes such as acquisitions and investments in new, lower-carbon energy solutions.

we are also decommissioning and divesting assets and reducing our production through the natural decline of existing oil and gas fields;

improving the energy efficiency of our operations;

transforming our remaining integrated refineries into low-carbon energy and chemicals parks, which involves decommissioning plants;

using more renewable electricity to power our operations;

developing carbon capture and storage (CCS) for our facilities;

reducing methane emissions.

We are also providing more lower-carbon energy solutions such as charging for electric vehicles, hydrogen and electricity generated by solar and wind power, and we are using technology to safely capture and store carbon emissions. For remaining emissions, we offer carbon credits including from nature-based projects.

We are working with our customers as they make changes too, including in areas of transport that are harder to decarbonise – such as aviation, shipping and road freight – as well as heavy industry.

Find out how we’re transforming low-carbon energy supply and demand across sectors

Powering Progress in action

See examples of how we are delivering on our strategy.

Generating shareholder value

Powering Progress generates value for our shareholders. It provides the financial strength to profitably transform our company, as we provide the energy the world needs today and transition to net-zero emissions

Powering lives

We power lives by providing the vital energy people need, championing inclusion and contributing to local communities.

Respecting nature

Our Powering Progress strategy means respecting nature by protecting the environment, reducing waste and making a positive contribution to biodiversity.

Our core values

Our core values of honesty, integrity and respect for people lie at the heart of all we do, combined with our relentless focus on safety.

Footnotes

1 Provided previously announced intention to exit from onshore Nigeria is realised.

2 Shell’s net carbon intensity is the average intensity, weighted by sales volume, of the energy products sold by Shell. It is tracked, measured and reported using our Net Carbon Footprint (NCF) methodology.

Legal Disclaimer

Cautionary Note

The companies in which Shell plc directly and indirectly owns investments are separate legal entities. In this web page “Shell”, “Shell Group” and “Group” are sometimes used for convenience where references are made to Shell plc and its subsidiaries in general. Likewise, the words “we”, “us” and “our” are also used to refer to Shell plc and its subsidiaries in general or to those who work for them. These terms are also used where no useful purpose is served by identifying the particular entity or entities. ‘‘Subsidiaries’’, “Shell subsidiaries” and “Shell companies” as used in this web page refer to entities over which Shell plc either directly or indirectly has control. Entities and unincorporated arrangements over which Shell has joint control are generally referred to as “joint ventures” and “joint operations”, respectively. “Joint ventures” and “joint operations” are collectively referred to as “joint arrangements”. Entities over which Shell has significant influence but neither control nor joint control are referred to as “associates”. The term “Shell interest” is used for convenience to indicate the direct and/or indirect ownership interest held by Shell in an entity or unincorporated joint arrangement, after exclusion of all third-party interest.

Forward-Looking Statements

This web page contains forward-looking statements (within the meaning of the U.S. Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995) concerning the financial condition, results of operations and businesses of Shell. All statements other than statements of historical fact are, or may be deemed to be, forward-looking statements. Forward-looking statements are statements of future expectations that are based on management’s current expectations and assumptions and involve known and unknown risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results, performance or events to differ materially from those expressed or implied in these statements. Forward-looking statements include, among other things, statements concerning the potential exposure of Shell to market risks and statements expressing management’s expectations, beliefs, estimates, forecasts, projections and assumptions. These forward-looking statements are identified by their use of terms and phrases such as “aim”, “ambition”, ‘‘anticipate’’, ‘‘believe’’, ‘‘could’’, ‘‘estimate’’, ‘‘expect’’, ‘‘goals’’, ‘‘intend’’, ‘‘may’’, “milestones”, ‘‘objectives’’, ‘‘outlook’’, ‘‘plan’’, ‘‘probably’’, ‘‘project’’, ‘‘risks’’, “schedule”, ‘‘seek’’, ‘‘should’’, ‘‘target’’, ‘‘will’’ and similar terms and phrases. There are a number of factors that could affect the future operations of Shell and could cause those results to differ materially from those expressed in the forward-looking statements included in this web page, including (without limitation): (a) price fluctuations in crude oil and natural gas; (b) changes in demand for Shell’s products; (c) currency fluctuations; (d) drilling and production results; (e) reserves estimates; (f) loss of market share and industry competition; (g) environmental and physical risks; (h) risks associated with the identification of suitable potential acquisition properties and targets, and successful negotiation and completion of such transactions; (i) the risk of doing business in developing countries and countries subject to international sanctions; (j) legislative, judicial, fiscal and regulatory developments including regulatory measures addressing climate change; (k) economic and financial market conditions in various countries and regions; (l) political risks, including the risks of expropriation and renegotiation of the terms of contracts with governmental entities, delays or advancements in the approval of projects and delays in the reimbursement for shared costs; (m) risks associated with the impact of pandemics, such as the COVID-19 (coronavirus) outbreak, regional conflicts, such as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and a significant cybersecurity breach; and (n) changes in trading conditions. No assurance is provided that future dividend payments will match or exceed previous dividend payments. All forward-looking statements contained in this web page are expressly qualified in their entirety by the cautionary statements contained or referred to in this section. Readers should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements. Additional risk factors that may affect future results are contained in Shell plc’s Form 20-F for the year ended December 31, 2022 (available at www.shell.com/investors/news-and-filings/sec-filings.html and www.sec.gov). These risk factors also expressly qualify all forward-looking statements contained in this web page and should be considered by the reader. Each forward-looking statement speaks only as of the date of this web page, 29 February 2024. Neither Shell plc nor any of its subsidiaries undertake any obligation to publicly update or revise any forward-looking statement as a result of new information, future events or other information. In light of these risks, results could differ materially from those stated, implied or inferred from the forward-looking statements contained in this web page.

Shell’s net carbon intensity

Also, in this web page we may refer to Shell’s “Net Carbon Intensity”, which includes Shell’s carbon emissions from the production of our energy products, our suppliers’ carbon emissions in supplying energy for that production and our customers’ carbon emissions associated with their use of the energy products we sell. Shell only controls its own emissions. The use of the term Shell’s “Net Carbon Intensity” is for convenience only and not intended to suggest these emissions are those of Shell plc or its subsidiaries.

Shell’s net-Zero Emissions Target

Shell’s operating plan, outlook and budgets are forecasted for a ten-year period and are updated every year. They reflect the current economic environment and what we can reasonably expect to see over the next ten years. Accordingly, they reflect our Scope 1, Scope 2 and Net Carbon Intensity (NCI) targets over the next ten years. However, Shell’s operating plans cannot reflect our 2050 net-zero emissions target and 2035 NCI target, as these targets are currently outside our planning period. In the future, as society moves towards net-zero emissions, we expect Shell’s operating plans to reflect this movement. However, if society is not net zero in 2050, as of today, there would be significant risk that Shell may not meet this target.

Shell expects to publish its 2024 Energy Transition Strategy on March 14, 2024, which will include an update on Shell’s energy transition strategy and set out Shell’s climate targets and ambitions for the future.

Forward Looking Non-GAAP measures

This web page may contain certain forward-looking non-GAAP measures such as cash capital expenditure and divestments. We are unable to provide a reconciliation of these forward-looking Non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP financial measures because certain information needed to reconcile those Non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP financial measures is dependent on future events some of which are outside the control of Shell, such as oil and gas prices, interest rates and exchange rates. Moreover, estimating such GAAP measures with the required precision necessary to provide a meaningful reconciliation is extremely difficult and could not be accomplished without unreasonable effort. Non-GAAP measures in respect of future periods which cannot be reconciled to the most comparable GAAP financial measure are calculated in a manner which is consistent with the accounting policies applied in Shell plc’s consolidated financial statements.

The contents of websites referred to in this web page do not form part of this web page.

We may have used certain terms, such as resources, in this web page that the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) strictly prohibits us from including in our filings with the SEC. Investors are urged to consider closely the disclosure in our Form 20-F, File No 1-32575, available on the SEC website www.sec.gov.

source.locator: Principle (d), 'Comparisons must be fair and meaningful'

evidence.quote: A comparative claim that a clothing range is now ‘greener’ is unlikely to be fair and meaningful on its own and risks misleading consumers.

source.name: SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard

evidence.quote: The Corporate Net-Zero Standard is the world’s first science-based framework for corporate net-zero target setting.
evidence.note: Under the Standard a validated net-zero target requires near-term (5 to 10 year) science-based targets, a long-term target to cut at least 90 percent of emissions across scopes 1, 2 and 3 by 2050 at the latest, and neutralisation of only the residual; SBTi validation is the recognised test of whether a corporate net-zero target is science-based.

ext.match_note: Claiming alignment/support of the 1.5°C Paris goal without SBTi-style validation.

argument.text: The claim states a specific numeric target (below 0.2%) and a specific outcome year (2022), and Shell's own assured Sustainability Report data confirms the intensity was well below that threshold, at 0.05% and 0.01%. The claim is stated as an intensity ratio rather than absolute tonnage, but that mirrors the target as originally set on the same page, so the metric is consistent with how the goal was framed.

The claim trumpets meeting a methane 'intensity' target while never mentioning absolute methane volumes, so a reader has no way to judge whether total methane released actually fell. Methane is only a small share of Shell's overall emissions footprint, yet the framing gives this narrow metric outsized prominence on the page. Shell's own later strategy document reportedly revises the 2023 figures slightly, suggesting the 2022 number presented here is not a stable, final figure.

The statement is transparent that refinery transformation 'involves decommissioning plants,' a specific and checkable admission that is not softened or hidden. This is one bullet within a longer list of parallel decarbonisation measures on the page, so it need not stand alone as a full account of Shell's refining strategy. No cited evidence in this dossier is verified to contradict the wording itself.

The claim gives a precise, checkable figure — 'over 90% of the total emissions reported' — directly tying Scope 3 to total reported emissions, which is exactly the kind of specific, falsifiable statement audits ask for. This same figure is repeated verbatim in Shell's own climate target FAQs, so the page is at minimum internally consistent rather than opportunistically inflated for this context. If accurate, the figure candidly identifies Scope 3 as the dominant share of the footprint, which is the opposite of hiding the ball on where the impact lies.

The phrase 'low-carbon energy and chemicals parks' is undefined and unquantified, letting readers assume a wholesale green conversion of refineries rather than a partial process that, by Shell's own admission elsewhere, includes outright divestment of at least one park and closure of units. The wording 'which involves decommissioning plants' softens what may in fact be site closures or sales into a generic operational detail, omitting the scale and location information a reasonable reader needs per the CMA's omission principle.

By stating Scope 3 accounts for 'over 90%' of reported emissions right next to the net-zero framing, the page correctly names where Shell's real climate impact lies, yet the only sourcing for this figure is Shell's own FAQ page (V1) — no independent, assured breakdown of Scope 1/2/3 exists to confirm it. This makes a materially important admission checkable only against Shell's own repeated say-so, which under the CMA Green Claims Code (K3) is exactly the kind of unverified figure that should not be presented as settled fact without independent corroboration.

The statement is a plain factual description of an offering, not a claim of neutrality or quality, and it is explicitly framed as covering only 'remaining emissions' after other decarbonisation measures listed on the page. The page names the category honestly—'carbon credits including from nature-based projects'—without asserting any specific verification standard, so it cannot be faulted for contradicting a standard it never invoked. Critics who fault the omission of quality detail (V13, V14, V17, V18) are arguing for a fuller disclosure, which is a fair ask, but that is different from showing the sentence itself is false.

'Supports this ambition' commits Shell to nothing measurable, yet it sits atop a page framing the company's entire climate story around 1.5°C. Independent analysis from the Transition Pathway Initiative finds Shell's own intensity targets track to over 2°C, and Carbon Brief notes Shell continues investing against the IEA's finding that no new oil-and-gas investment is needed on a 1.5°C pathway. A French court has already found that similar 'net zero'/climate terminology from an oil major misled consumers by omitting that the company's own plan diverged from Paris-aligned scientific recommendations while it kept expanding oil and gas investment.

Shell describes offering 'carbon credits including from nature-based projects' for 'remaining emissions' without disclosing any verification standard, quantity, or the share of total emissions these are meant to cover. This omission matters because Dutch advertising authorities (P3, P4) have already upheld rulings against Shell for similarly unsubstantiated offset-based neutrality claims, and independent research (V17) found Shell among companies obtaining three-quarters or more of its credits from stale, pre-2013 projects, while Climate Home News (V13, V14) reports Shell counting discredited credits toward its climate goals. Shell's own Sustainability Report reportedly qualifies these credits as 'high-quality' (S2), a caveat conspicuously absent from this page's phrasing, suggesting the public-facing claim is looser than the company's internal standard.

The 0.05% figure for facilities with marketed gas is directly corroborated by Shell's own assured performance table, which reports the identical figure. Both percentages are precise and give readers a checkable number rather than vague language, satisfying the basic function of a factual progress statement even though the non-marketed-gas figure lacks a directly shown assured source.

'more renewable electricity' is a comparative with no baseline, volume, or percentage, so a reader cannot check whether this is a token gesture or a substantial shift. It also does not disclose whether the renewable electricity is Shell's own generation or purchased certificates, a distinction the FTC Green Guides and GHG Protocol both treat as material to avoid misleading impressions of use.

The precise-looking 0.05%/0.01% split creates an impression of rigorous, fully-audited disclosure, but the dossier shows only the 0.05% marketed-gas figure is actually confirmed in Shell's assured performance table; the 0.01% non-marketed figure is unverified against any assured source. As with the related claim, intensity percentages omit absolute methane tonnage, so the reader cannot gauge real-world impact from these ratios alone.

The claim reports only two already-completed milestones (2-3% by 2021) within a longer disclosed staircase running to 2050, and Shell's later strategy update independently confirms the early-year figures cited as achieved. A target is not a promise of every future rung; the fact that later 2030/2035 figures were subsequently revised does not retroactively make the 2021 'achieved' claim false, since it concerns only that year's outcome.

The target states a specific percentage, a firm date, and an explicit 2016 baseline, which is precisely the kind of measurable, time-bound commitment regulators ask companies to publish. The 'net basis' qualifier is disclosed on the face of the claim rather than hidden in a footnote, giving readers the information needed to understand the metric. The 50%-by-2030 target and its scope are restated identically elsewhere, showing this is a stable, long-standing commitment rather than a one-off marketing flourish.

The claim that Shell is 'developing carbon capture and storage (CCS) for our facilities' presents CCS as an established, general solution without naming scale, timeline, or facility count. Shell's own later strategy materials reportedly cap CCS investment narrowly and note it lacks a clear business model in many countries, a qualification entirely absent from this page's confident framing.

The claim only states that Shell is 'working with' customers in hard-to-decarbonise sectors, a modest and inherently collaborative framing that does not promise Shell will single-handedly solve aviation, shipping or road-freight emissions. Shell's own aviation president is on record (V19) acknowledging that sustainable aviation fuel is under 0.1% of global use today, which is consistent with, not contradictory to, a claim of ongoing engagement rather than completed transformation. The ASA's most recent ruling on a related Shell ad (P23) was not upheld, indicating regulators have not found this kind of framing misleading in at least one comparable instance.

The '50% by 2030... on a net basis' target sounds like a hard operational cut, but the qualifier 'net basis' quietly allows offsets or accounting adjustments to count toward the figure, obscuring what portion is genuine abatement. Worse, Shell's own reporting (V5) indicates a large share of the already-achieved 30% cut came from divesting and shutting down assets rather than decarbonising them — a dynamic the page's forward 50% target does not disclose, even though continuing to divest rather than abate would let Shell hit the number without equivalent emissions reductions occurring elsewhere. Since this target only covers Scope 1 and 2, which the page's own admission (C7) puts at under 10% of total emissions, its prominence is disproportionate to its share of real climate impact.

The phrase 'working with our customers as they make changes too' diffuses responsibility for decarbonising aviation, shipping, road freight and heavy industry onto unnamed customer actions without specifying Shell's own contribution. Yet Shell's own aviation president is quoted admitting that sustainable aviation fuel — the flagship example of this 'work' — accounts for 'less than 0.1% of the world's use of aviation fuel' (V19), making the vague language of partnership materially disproportionate to the sectors named. This gap between the sweeping framing and the negligible real-world penetration in the very sectors cited creates a misleading impression of substantive progress.

The unqualified 2050 net-zero target implies a settled, achievable commitment, but Carbon Brief reports Shell has already retired its 2035 intensity target due to 'uncertainty in the pace of change,' and ClientEarth notes Shell fails the Climate Action 100+ Benchmark test requiring net-zero-aligned short, medium and long-term targets across all relevant emissions. The ASA has previously upheld a complaint against Shell for exactly this kind of omission, finding that ads giving the impression of a low-carbon business model needed to disclose the proportion of Shell's overall business that was actually lower-carbon. Carbon Tracker further notes the 'net zero by 2050' headline that readers naturally associate with the whole business actually applies only to Shell's own operations, not the products it sells.

Labelling '2-3% by 2021' as 'achieved' presents a settled, verified fact, yet no independently assured dataset for 2021 net carbon intensity was found in the dossier—only 2022 data carries assurance. More seriously, Shell's own later strategy update reportedly revised the 2030 figure downward and dropped the 2035 rung of this very ladder, meaning the 'achieved' early milestones are presented as part of a stable staircase that the company itself did not keep intact.

The line names concrete mechanisms — acquisitions, investments in lower-carbon solutions — as part of a longer, itemised list of specific levers used elsewhere on the page, giving readers a checkable set of actions rather than an empty assertion. Shell's own later strategy document restates this same bullet essentially unchanged, showing the description is consistent with the company's ongoing account of its approach.

The bare bullet 'reducing methane emissions' carries no quantity, baseline, or date, leaving readers to assume a significant and open-ended reduction effort. The CMA's omission principle requires that important context—like the specific intensity figures reported elsewhere on the page—not be left out of a claim placed alongside other operational bullets.

The phrase 'using more renewable electricity' is a plain, checkable directional claim about operational power sourcing, not a comparative percentage claim requiring a baseline to be true. It sits among several other listed operational measures, so it is offered as one input among many rather than the whole decarbonisation story. No evidence in the dossier establishes that Shell's renewable electricity use fails the sourcing quality standards cited.

Shell states plainly that CCS is being 'developed,' language that itself signals an in-progress technology rather than a claim of current large-scale deployment, so readers are not told it is already solving the bulk of emissions. The bullet is one item in a list of several decarbonisation levers, not presented as the primary solution. The alleged contradictions from later strategy documents rest on unverified quotes and cannot be relied upon to show inconsistency.

The claim states a specific, dated, scoped commitment — eliminate routine flaring from upstream operations by 2025 — and Shell's later pages confirm this target was in fact met, with effect from January 2025. The Nigeria-exit caveat is disclosed, even if only in a footnote, meaning the qualification is present on the page rather than omitted entirely. That the target was subsequently reported as achieved (S24) supports the credibility of the original commitment.

This sentence frames Shell as personally ensuring emissions are 'balanced by removal,' but ClientEarth documents that Shell explicitly disclaims responsibility for the emissions caused by use of its own products, stating 'Shell only controls its own emissions.' The passive construction 'balanced by removal' obscures who is actually responsible for balancing the emissions Shell's products generate, letting the aspirational language imply a completeness the company elsewhere disavows.

The words say only that 'Shell supports this ambition,' a plain statement of position on the global 1.5°C goal, not a claim that Shell's own targets are independently verified as 1.5°C-aligned. The wording is a weak verb by design, expressing endorsement of an ambition rather than asserting achievement or alignment, so it cannot be tested against intensity-pathway modelling as if it promised alignment. Critics cited in the dossier (V6, V10) address Shell's investment pattern and intensity targets, not this specific sentence of support for the UN-level ambition.

The claim promises to 'eliminate routine flaring... by 2025' but omits from the visible text the Nigeria-exit condition, burying it in footnote 1, so a reasonable reader sees an unconditional commitment where one does not fully exist. Shell's own later material (V3) confirms the target was called achieved from January 2025, but this is company self-reporting with no independent verification that the footnoted precondition was actually satisfied at the time.

The phrase 'lower-carbon energy solutions' sets no baseline or standard, letting virtually any acquisition qualify as progress. Shell's own FAQ page states the fuller version of this same bullet includes 'while sustaining our liquids production,' a qualifier the audited page conspicuously omits, leaving readers with the impression that portfolio changes are purely decarbonising rather than paired with continued oil and gas output.

This is a values statement introducing the 'Respecting nature' section, situated alongside similarly worded sections like 'Powering lives' and 'Our core values,' signalling to a reasonable reader that it is a summary strategic theme rather than a quantified metric. The phrase does not claim zero environmental harm, only that the strategy 'means' protecting the environment, reducing waste and contributing to biodiversity, which are directional aims consistent with the detailed operational and emissions targets given elsewhere on the same page. No evidence in this dossier shows the sentence itself asserts a false fact; the objection is that it lacks quantification, which is a clarity critique rather than a demonstration of a false statement.

This is a plain, factual description of concrete and easily verifiable actions — decommissioning, divesting, and natural field decline — not a claim of climate benefit in itself. It is presented as one item in a list of measures rather than as a standalone environmental achievement, and Shell's later strategy document repeats the same bullet with the same scope, indicating this is a stable and consistently described part of its operations.

The claim that Powering Progress means 'respecting nature by protecting the environment, reducing waste and making a positive contribution to biodiversity' uses undefined slogans with no measurable proposition, matching the generic environmental-benefit language flagged by regulatory guidance (K1, K5, K9, K14). An ASA ruling against Innocent (P15) found nearly identical unqualified positive-impact claims misleading, and ClientEarth's reporting (V18) shows that biodiversity-linked offset projects Shell relies on elsewhere can themselves cause the negative biodiversity impacts this claim disclaims. The unqualified phrasing thus creates an impression of net positive stewardship unsupported by specific, verifiable evidence.

Listing electric vehicle charging, hydrogen, and solar/wind electricity as things Shell is 'providing more' of, without any share-of-business figure, mirrors the exact framing the ASA found misleading against Shell itself: giving the impression that lower-carbon products are a significant part of the business while omitting the proportion of the business that remains fossil-based. The ASA's Repsol ruling reinforces that omitting the role and scale of such lower-carbon offerings in the overall plan is material to consumers' understanding.

'Reducing methane emissions' is a bare factual bullet, but the page elsewhere gives it real teeth: it reports methane intensity of 0.05% and 0.01% for 2022 against a stated 0.2% target, which is checkable data supporting the general direction claimed. The bullet is not asked to carry quantitative weight on its own since the specifics appear nearby on the same page.

The 'below 0.2%' methane intensity ceiling is stated without the asset-scope qualifier that Shell's own FAQ page (V2) attaches — 'operated oil and gas assets' — so the page presents a broader-sounding commitment than the one Shell actually measures against. As an intensity rather than absolute metric, it also lets total methane emissions rise alongside production growth while still meeting the stated target.

The claim sets a clear, numeric intensity ceiling with a firm date, which is a specific, falsifiable commitment. Later company reporting restates the same target and scope, showing consistent use of this metric across time rather than a figure adjusted to suit this particular page. The underlying performance data, drawn from the company's own reporting, shows results well below the stated ceiling, consistent with the target being a genuine constraint rather than an empty aspiration.

The claim that Shell's target 'supports' the Paris 1.5°C goal is undercut by the Transition Pathway Initiative's finding that Shell's own 2025 and 2030 intensity targets track to over 2°C of warming, and by Carbon Brief's reporting that Shell has already abandoned its 2035 target. ClientEarth further notes Shell fails the Climate Action 100+ Benchmark for lacking net-zero-aligned targets across short, medium and long term horizons, which cuts against implying the whole trajectory 'supports' Paris.

This bullet is folded into a list under a decarbonisation heading, but divestment and natural field decline are asset and production changes, not emissions reductions Shell's operations actually achieve through cleaner technology. The dossier's own note suggests this lever may be the dominant driver behind the reported 30% operational emissions cut, meaning the page's framing risks crediting 'decarbonisation' for what is largely portfolio shrinkage rather than genuine operational improvement.

The statement claims a direction of travel — improving efficiency — without quantifying it, but it is offered as one line in a longer list of levers, not as a headline metric requiring precision. Shell's own data shows the upstream energy-intensity figure moving from 1.19 down to 1.06 GJ/tonne across the reported years, a net improvement over the period even if not monotonic every year, which supports the general direction claimed.

Saying Shell is 'using technology to safely capture and store carbon emissions' names no specific technology, volume, or facility and so cannot be checked against Shell's actual CCS footprint. Shell's own later strategy report reportedly caps CCS spending and focuses it mainly on Shell's own operations rather than the broad, customer-facing impression this generic sentence creates.

The claim states a specific target and date — net-zero by 2050 — and the very next paragraphs on the page define its scope as covering Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, so the term is not left hanging undefined for long. The page also reports concrete interim progress toward the goal, including a stated 30% reduction in operational emissions by 2022 against a 2016 baseline, giving readers a checkable trajectory rather than a bare promise. It is fair to concede that a 2050 target inherently depends on conditions the company cannot control, but stating a dated, scoped target with reported interim progress is a specific and checkable commitment on its own terms.

This claim precisely and narrowly names Scope 1 and 2 as the operational net-zero boundary, and Carbon Tracker's independent reporting confirms that Shell's 'net zero' language does in fact apply only to operational emissions — so the wording matches reality here rather than misleading. The dossier gives no case for deception on this specific sub-claim.

This is a forward-looking target for 2030, and a target is not a promise of present performance; the claim does not assert that near-zero methane has already been achieved. The same near-zero-by-2030 methane framing is repeated in Shell's later Annual Report, showing this is a maintained, non-contradicted commitment rather than a claim quietly abandoned elsewhere.

'Near-zero' by 2030 is an undefined term with no numeric threshold given anywhere on the page, so a reader cannot check what level of methane emissions would satisfy or fail this commitment. Under the EU's forward-looking claims criteria (K6), a claim about future environmental performance without a clear, verifiable, time-bound target is precisely the kind of language that creates a false impression of concreteness.

The claim lists concrete, named product categories — EV charging, hydrogen, solar and wind electricity — which are specific and checkable examples rather than vague assertions. It is phrased as 'providing more,' a modest directional claim about growth in these offerings rather than a claim these dominate Shell's business, and the ASA finding concerned different ads' overall impression, not necessarily this page's wording.

The claim asserts a simple upward trajectory of 'improving' energy efficiency, but Shell's own assured performance data shows a mixed trend, including at least one period where upstream energy intensity increased rather than improved. No baseline or quantity accompanies the claim, so readers cannot check the vague assertion against the actual numbers Shell reports elsewhere.

This sentence is explicitly aspirational — 'We want to contribute to a net-zero world' — and does not purport to be a quantified, standalone commitment; the hedge is visible on the page itself, not hidden. Read alongside the immediately following paragraph, which sets out the concrete, dated net-zero-by-2050 target, this sentence functions as scene-setting rather than the operative pledge, so it should not be judged as if it were the measurable target itself.

This is a general statement of intent about capture-and-store technology within a longer list of measures; it does not claim CCS resolves the majority of Shell's emissions, so its materiality should be judged against that modest framing. The suggestion that later strategy documents cap CCS spending does not contradict this page, since a capped investment is still consistent with 'using technology' at some real scale, and those later quotes are unverified in any case.

The 30% figure is precise and checkable, but the page presents it as unqualified progress toward decarbonisation while Shell's own Energy Transition Progress Report (V5) indicates a substantial share of that cut came from divesting and shutting down assets rather than from operational abatement. Presenting a divestment-driven number alongside operational efficiency measures listed elsewhere on the page creates the impression of a company that is decarbonising its operations when much of the reduction may simply reflect owning less of the emitting assets.

The claim states a specific percentage, baseline year and scope (operations), making it directly checkable, and this exact 30% figure is corroborated in Shell's own Sustainability Report and Form 20-F filing for the same period. The claim is presented as historical progress toward the separately-stated 2030 target, not as a claim that the job is finished. Later reporting shows the same metric continuing to move (36% by 2025 against the same 2016 baseline), consistent with ongoing, non-contradictory progress reporting rather than a figure at odds with the company's later record.

Framing Scope 3 net-zero as covering 'all the energy products we sell' implies comprehensive coverage, yet ClientEarth's analysis reportedly finds Shell's Scope 3 net-zero commitment excludes its petrochemicals business, and Shell's own 20-F reportedly contains only one concrete Scope 3 metric: a 15-20% reduction 'ambition' limited to oil products by 2030, far narrower than a full net-zero-by-2050 commitment across everything sold. The ASA upheld a near-identical complaint against Repsol for failing to contextualize how and when a net-zero claim would actually be achieved, which is the same gap here between the sweeping 'all' and the narrower substantiated commitment.

The claim uses 'supports' deliberately, asserting that Shell's target is directed at the same broader goal as the Paris Agreement, not that Shell's plan has been certified as delivering 1.5°C outcomes. This is consistent with the wording elsewhere on the page, which frames the 2050 net-zero target and the 50% Scope 1/2 reduction by 2030 as company commitments in support of, rather than equivalent to, the Paris temperature goal. It is fair to note that outside analyses (V9, V10) question whether Shell's specific intensity trajectory is Paris-aligned, but that is a critique of the underlying targets, not evidence that the sentence itself misstates what it claims to do.

This is the most precisely scoped sentence on the page: it names the exact boundary — Scope 1 and Scope 2, i.e. Shell's own operations — for its net-zero claim, rather than leaving the term open-ended. Independent commentary in the dossier (V16) corroborates that Shell's 'net zero' language does in fact apply to operational emissions, which supports rather than undermines the accuracy of this specific, narrowly drawn statement. The claim's materiality is limited given operations are a small share of total footprint, but that is a matter of scope, not of the sentence being inaccurate about what it covers.

The sentence explicitly names its scope as Scope 3 emissions from 'the end use of all the energy products we sell,' which is more specific than a bare 'net zero' claim and directs the reader to the reported metric basis. It should be conceded that independent commentary (V15) notes Shell separately states it does not control customers' emissions, and that the concrete Scope 3 metric elsewhere is narrower than 'all' products, so the word 'all' overstates the boundary of what is actually measured and managed.
